history.heading: Island and mainland
paragraphs: Equatorial Guinea consists of a mainland region, Río Muni, between Cameroon and Gabon, and islands including Bioko, where the capital Malabo lies, and Annobón. Bioko was settled by the Bubi people, while the Fang are the largest group on the mainland.

Portuguese navigator Fernão do Pó reached Bioko in the 1470s. Portugal ceded the territories to Spain in 1778. Britain used Bioko as a base against the slave trade in the 19th century. Under Spanish rule, cocoa plantations on Bioko used contract labour from other parts of Africa.

history.heading: Independence and dictatorship
paragraphs: Equatorial Guinea became independent from Spain on 12 October 1968. Its first president, Francisco Macías Nguema, established one of Africa's most brutal dictatorships; a large part of the population was killed or fled.

His nephew Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo overthrew and executed him in 1979 and has ruled ever since, making him the world's longest-serving non-royal head of state. The discovery of oil in the 1990s transformed the economy.

culture.heading: Languages and traditions
paragraphs: Equatorial Guinea is the only African country with Spanish as an official language; French and Portuguese are also official. Fang, Bubi and other languages are widely spoken. Most people are Catholic.
Traditional music and dance include the balélé and the Fang mvet, an epic storytelling tradition accompanied by a harp-zither.

politics.heading: Authoritarian rule
paragraphs: Equatorial Guinea is formally a presidential republic, but power is concentrated in President Obiang, his family and his Democratic Party of Equatorial Guinea, which wins elections with overwhelming majorities. His son Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue is vice-president. Opposition activity and press freedom are severely restricted, and the family has faced corruption cases abroad.

economy.heading: Oil wealth and poverty
paragraphs: Oil and gas, discovered in the 1990s, account for nearly all exports and made Equatorial Guinea one of Africa's richest countries per person on paper. However, wealth is highly concentrated, and much of the population lives in poverty with limited access to services.
Declining oil production has caused economic contraction. The currency is the Central African CFA franc.
